operationalization: For continental and near-continental islands, regress terrestrial-mammal species sharing and mean phylogenetic distance to the nearest mainland on minimum intervening sea depth, with geographic distance and island area held constant. The claim is confirmed if greater depth still predicts fewer shared species and more distant allies, and refuted if depth adds no partial association or the slope reverses.

candidate_datasets.name: GEBCO
candidate_datasets.role: Gridded global bathymetry for the minimum sea depth of channels between islands and the nearest mainland.

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: Range maps of terrestrial mammals used to score species shared between an island and the neighbouring mainland.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level mammal phylogeny for measuring how closely allied island and mainland mammals are.

obstacles: Modern depth is an imperfect stand-in for Pleistocene land connections, because channels shallower than past lowstands were periodically dry.
Introduced mammals and incomplete native inventories can inflate or deflate apparent sharing.
Island area, climate and human history remain confounded with depth even after distance is controlled.
rationale: Depth, distance, species lists and phylogenetic relatedness are standard variables, and the partial-regression criterion follows the claim's 'independent of distance' wording directly. Open bathymetry, mammal range maps and a dated mammal tree cover most continental islands, with weaker native-status data for small islands. The comparison is a routine spatial analysis, though land-bridge history and introductions keep it from being fully clean.

operationalization: For oceanic-island endemics, compare phylogenetic distance to relatives on the nearest continent or nearby islands with distance to biotas in climatically more similar but geographically farther regions. The claim is confirmed if nearest-source relatives are closer in a large majority of well-sampled clades, and refuted if climate-matching distant regions win about as often.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence records used to assign endemic island taxa and candidate source regions.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Synthetic phylogeny for placing island endemics relative to continental relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: WorldClim
candidate_datasets.role: Climate layers for identifying distant regions whose physical conditions resemble an island more than the nearest mainland does.

obstacles: Most invertebrate and many plant endemics are still missing from phylogenetic trees, so the testable set is biased toward vertebrates and well-studied floras.
Extinct source populations on the nearest continent can make a living relative look farther away than the historical source.
Ocean currents and wind can make the biologically accessible source differ from the nearest shoreline.
rationale: Nearest-continent versus climate-matched distant region is a direct decision rule, and public occurrences, climate layers and a synthetic tree supply the variables for well-studied archipelagos. Coverage falls well short of every endemic plant and animal, so the 'almost universal' scope is only partly in reach. Where trees and inventories exist, multiple colonizations and missing mainland sisters are manageable biases rather than fatal ones.

operationalization: Within each oceanic archipelago, test whether endemic species on different islands are reciprocally closer, or form a single clade, relative to species from every other region. The claim is confirmed if within-archipelago phylogenetic distances are consistently the shortest, and refuted if closest relatives usually lie outside the archipelago.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic placement of island endemics to compare within-archipelago and external relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public sequences for rebuilding clade trees where the synthetic tree is poorly resolved.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Locality records used to assign endemics to islands within an archipelago.

obstacles: Unsampled continental relatives can make an archipelago radiation look monophyletic when it is not.
Many endemic invertebrates and plants have no sequences, so existing trees over-represent famous radiations.
Repeated colonizations of the same archipelago are a real biological alternative and require dense geographic sampling to detect.
rationale: Monophyly, or shorter within-archipelago distances, is a standard phylogenetic criterion and matches the claim without much reinterpretation. Sequence archives and occurrence data support that test for many vertebrates and some plants, and leave most of the world's island endemics unplaced. The analysis itself is ordinary; assembling a taxonomically balanced sample is what pushes the work beyond a quick study.

operationalization: For regional floras and faunas, compare the phylogenetic distance of naturalised species to the native biota, and the fraction whose genus is absent from the natives, against a null draw from the pool of species that could have been introduced. The claim is confirmed if successful naturalisations are concentrated in genera missing from the region, and refuted if they are as closely allied to natives as the introduction pool.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: Global lists of naturalised alien plant species by region, for comparison with native floras.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distances between naturalised species and the native species of the recipient region.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Introduced-status occurrences that extend the same comparison from plants to animals.

obstacles: Humans preferentially transport particular families, so an apparent excess of distinct genera can be an introduction bias.
The result depends on how the source pool is defined, including which species had the opportunity to be moved.
Animal naturalisation inventories are less complete and less standardised than the plant compilation.
rationale: Genus absence and phylogenetic distance to natives are measurable readings of 'not closely allied', and global naturalised-plant lists already tabulate the main botanical pattern Darwin cited. Animal coverage is thinner, but introduced-status occurrences are public and the same test applies. The analysis is standard and has been run before; transport bias and source-pool choice are the reasons discriminating power stays moderate.

operationalization: For islands, sky-islands, lakes and caves, compare the phylogenetic source region of endemics with a dispersal-accessibility model based on distance and barriers, and score whether colonists are phenotypically shifted toward local conditions. The claim is confirmed if the best-supported source matches the most accessible region and derived populations are more environment-matched than their source relatives, and refuted if sources are random with respect to access or phenotypes are unchanged.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenies used to infer source regions of isolated biotas.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences of island, mountain, lake and cave taxa and of their candidate source biotas.

candidate_datasets.name: Map of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Expert range maps that complement occurrence records for identifying accessible source regions.

obstacles: 'Most readily' requires a dispersal model, and currents, bird vectors and past climates give several competing versions.
Being related to a source shows colonisation, while 'better fitted' needs trait-environment data that most of these biotas lack.
Cave, marsh and lake endemics are inventoried far more unevenly than oceanic islands.
rationale: The colonisation half can be turned into a source-region test, but accessibility and subsequent adaptation each admit several operationalizations, which lowers the score. Phylogenies and range data cover classic islands much better than caves, marshes and alpine lakes. A broad multi-habitat analysis would take months of harmonization, and adaptation remains a proxy rather than a fitness measurement.

operationalization: Across pairs of bioregions, count shared species, sister or congeneric pairs, and taxa with unstable species-versus-variety rank, then test whether regions rich in allied pairs also share some identical species and more borderline taxa. The claim is confirmed if that joint pattern is nearly general after controlling for region size and survey effort, and refuted if many region pairs have numerous allied species and no shared species.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Species-by-region occurrence matrices for counting shared and unshared taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A common taxonomy for scoring identical species, congeners and rank-unstable names.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic proximity used to identify allied or representative species pairs independently of genus names.

obstacles: Taxonomists already split and lump borderline forms most actively where regions share related biotas, so 'doubtful forms' partly reflect effort.
A few very widespread species can create shared-species counts without any special history of migration.
Survey effort and species concepts differ sharply between regions, which can manufacture or hide the predicted association.
rationale: Shared species, close relatives and nomenclatural borderline cases can be counted from public checklists and trees, so the pattern is operational for vertebrates and seed plants. The universal wording is only as strong as taxonomic practice, which uses the same gaps the claim is about. The analysis is feasible at bioregion scale, with serious circularity around how species and varieties are ranked.

operationalization: Using an explicit proxy for 'lower', such as non-seed plants versus seed plants or small-bodied versus large-bodied animals, compare geographic range size or number of regions occupied. The claim is confirmed if the lower proxy has systematically larger ranges after correcting for the number of records, and refuted if range size is unrelated to that proxy or runs the other way.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence extents used as a range-size measure across animals and plants.

candidate_datasets.name: GIFT
candidate_datasets.role: Regional floras for comparing how widely bryophytes, pteridophytes and seed plants are distributed.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A taxonomic backbone for assigning groups to the chosen higher-versus-lower proxy.

obstacles: 'Lower in the scale of nature' has several competing modern proxies, and they do not rank the same organisms together.
Recorded ranges of microbes and minute invertebrates are dominated by where people have sampled, not by where the organisms live.
Better-studied large organisms can look either more or less widespread depending on whether range is measured as a map or as a list of records.
rationale: The sentence has a measurable biogeographic pattern only after 'lower' is replaced by a grade, body size or propagule size, and those mappings disagree. Checklist and occurrence databases can support a proxy test inside plants or vertebrates and cannot support one across all of life. Sampling bias is large enough that many outcomes would still be compatible with both the claim and its opposite.

operationalization: Across living and fossil species, test whether phylogenetic distance increases with geographic distance and with separation in time, using divergence dates or stratigraphic midpoints. The claim is confirmed if both partial associations are positive across large clades, and refuted if close relatives are no nearer in space or time than distant relatives once sampling effort is controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distances among living taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence centroids or ranges for geographic separation among relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences and ages for temporal and geographic separation among extinct forms.

obstacles: Geography has historically influenced which specimens taxonomists treat as separate species, which can tighten the spatial pattern by construction.
Fossil finds are concentrated in well-worked basins, so apparent closeness in time and space partly tracks rock exposure.
Molecular divergence dates are model-based proxies for the temporal nearness Darwin described from fossils and living ranges.
rationale: Phylogenetic, geographic and temporal distances are ordinary variables, and a positive partial association is an obvious confirming result for a claim qualified by 'generally'. Public trees, occurrences and fossil occurrences cover enough clades to accept or reject that general tendency, even though most fossil species lack a resolved phylogeny. Sampling bias is serious and is the reason discriminating power is not higher.

operationalization: Ask whether character data from living and fossil organisms fit a branching hierarchy better than non-hierarchical or highly reticulate alternatives, and whether extinction of intermediate branches is required to reproduce the observed gaps between named groups. The claim is confirmed if tree-like structure is strong and simulated divergence without extinction of intermediates fails to produce the observed rank gaps, and refuted if the data are poorly hierarchical or gaps arise without that extinction.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Sequence matrices for measuring how hierarchical living diversity is, against network-like alternatives.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global tree summarizing which groups are nested inside which.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil ranges used to ask whether extinct intermediates occupy the gaps between living groups.

obstacles: A pure branching process produces nested groups even when extinction is random, so the specific role of exterminating less divergent forms is hard to isolate.
Building a tree and then reading nested groups off it is circular unless the test is a fit comparison against non-tree models.
Horizontal transfer, hybridization and uneven fossil recovery all reduce the clarity of the hierarchy.
rationale: Nested taxonomy is visible in existing trees, but the claim is a mechanism, and several branching models produce the same nesting. Sequence archives and the fossil record can test tree-likeness and the presence of extinct intermediates, which is only part of the causal story. A careful model comparison is feasible for major clades and does not cleanly separate this mechanism from simpler alternatives.

operationalization: Compare traditional classifications with independently estimated molecular trees and ask whether closeness of descent predicts classificatory grouping beyond raw similarity. The claim is confirmed if classifications recover phylogenetic proximity after phenotypic similarity is accounted for, and refuted if they track overall resemblance or ecological similarity instead.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: An independent phylogenetic target for what classifications ought to recover if they track descent.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Current named groups whose nesting can be compared with the tree.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular characters that are largely separate from the morphological resemblance traditional classifications used.

obstacles: What naturalists 'seek' in a natural system is a historical intention, not a column in a dataset.
Gene transfer and convergence also generate similarity, so descent is not the only measurable cause.
Many ranks were revised after molecular trees existed, so congruence with those trees is partly by later construction.
rationale: Congruence between molecular trees and named groups is a real empirical core, and the needed trees and classifications are public. The wording also makes a conceptual claim about the hidden bond of the Natural System and about descent as the only cause of similarity, which those databases do not settle. The feasible analysis therefore tests a proxy, phylogenetic concordance, rather than the claim in full.

operationalization: In morphological matrices, partition characters into those tied to special habits and those that are structural, then compare their constancy across large clades and their phylogenetic signal at deep nodes. The claim is confirmed if habit-linked characters are less conserved and less informative for higher groups, and refuted if they are as constant as, or more constant than, structural characters.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published character matrices in which habit-linked and structural characters can be separated.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees on which constancy and deep-node signal of each character class can be measured.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant traits linked to habitat and life form, as a functional contrast to conserved floral and anatomical characters.

obstacles: Deciding that a character has been 'little modified by adaptation' is itself an interpretation and will differ among coders.
Systematists already prefer constant characters, so high classificatory value is partly how the matrices were assembled.
Public matrices cover a minority of animal and plant groups, with a strong bias toward vertebrates.
rationale: Constancy and deep phylogenetic signal are measurable, but the adaptive status of a character is not a standard column and has to be assigned. Existing matrices and trait databases support the comparison in scattered taxa, especially vertebrates and some plant families. Harmonizing those matrices and coding function would take months, and the coding step limits how decisive the result can be.

operationalization: For genera, families and orders, measure the spread of crown ages, species richness and morphological disparity within each rank, and test whether ranks occupy distinct, non-overlapping bands. The claim is confirmed if within-rank spreads dwarf the differences between adjacent ranks, and refuted if a rank consistently marks a similar age or amount of difference across classes.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Divergence times for comparing crown ages of taxa that share a Linnaean rank.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Current assignment of clades to genus, family, order and similar ranks.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global hierarchy used to place ranked names on a common tree and to count species per clade.

obstacles: 'Almost arbitrary' has no sharp numerical cutoff, so a weak average rise in age from genus to order can be read either way.
Ranks are more nearly commensurate inside one class than they are across animals and plants together.
Some rank changes really do follow the discovery of more allied species, but the historical revision record is less complete than the current ages.
rationale: Rank, clade age and richness are standard variables, and massive overlap within a rank versus a clean age band is a concrete confirming or refuting pattern. Time-calibrated trees and a global taxonomy already contain those variables for most named higher taxa. The analysis is a short one; the remaining softness is the vague word 'almost', not missing data.

operationalization: For sister clades, which are equally related to their common ancestor, compare phenotypic disparity or morphological branch length and the Linnaean ranks later assigned to each side. The claim is confirmed if equally close branches often differ several-fold in accumulated modification, and refuted if sister clades are consistently similar in amount of change.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Sister-clade pairs of equal age against which unequal amounts of change can be judged.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Large species-level trees for vertebrates, where unequal rates among sister clades can be estimated.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices for measuring phenotypic modification separately from molecular branch length.

obstacles: The requirement that a natural arrangement must be genealogical is a rule for classification, and datasets do not test the word 'must'.
Molecular branch lengths are abundant, while the amount of bodily modification Darwin meant is available only where morphological matrices exist.
Rank differences between sister clades partly record later taxonomic taste rather than a measured quantity of change.
rationale: Unequal modification of sister lineages is directly measurable, and public trees make the sister-clade design straightforward for vertebrates. The genealogical 'must' in the same sentence is normative, so existing data test the empirical half. Morphological coverage is the main limit on adequacy, and the rate comparison itself is a standard phylogenetic analysis.

operationalization: For domestic breeds and wild varieties with known pedigrees or genomic relationships, test whether morphology and named subgroups form a nested hierarchy that matches descent, with deeper splits corresponding to greater modification. The claim is confirmed if breed groups recover the pedigree better than a non-hierarchical clustering, and refuted if varieties of known close descent are morphologically scattered among distant breeds.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Public breed and variety genomes that record pedigree independent of the traits used to name the breeds.

candidate_datasets.name: DAD-IS
candidate_datasets.role: Global inventory of domestic breeds whose named hierarchy can be compared with genetic descent.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic context for wild varieties and the species that contain them.

obstacles: Breeds were often defined by the same external traits used to test nested morphological groups, which makes a purely morphological test circular.
Genomic pedigrees are dense for dogs, horses, chickens and a few crops, and sparse for most domesticated and wild varieties.
Wild 'varieties' are delimited inconsistently, so the natural-variety half of the scope is much weaker than the breed half.
rationale: Where pedigrees exist, nested breed groups can be compared with descent without adopting a new definition of variety. Public genomes and breed inventories cover a few domesticated species well and leave most wild varieties out, so only a restricted scope is testable. Genomic data break the circularity of testing morphology with groups that morphology defined, at the cost of months of cross-study harmonization.

operationalization: Code characters shared by many ecologically dissimilar species and ask whether those characters, including rudiments, match an independent molecular tree more often than characters shared by species with similar habits. The claim is confirmed if cross-habit characters are phylogenetically conserved and habit-linked similarities are homoplasious, and refuted if the reverse holds.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices that record which traits are shared across species with different habits.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular trees used as an independent standard for common inheritance.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Habit and habitat traits for separating ecological similarity from shared structure in plants.

obstacles: Developmental constraint and gene transfer can spread a character across dissimilar species without inheritance from the group's common parent.
Habit categories in matrices are coarse, so 'very different habits' is only approximately known.
Rudimentary structures are mentioned sporadically in anatomical matrices rather than scored across whole classes.
rationale: The contrast between cross-habit characters and habit-linked resemblances is a usable test of homology versus convergence, once habits are coded. Matrices and molecular trees exist for many vertebrate groups and some plants, not for animals and plants at large. The analysis is standard cladistic fit, slowed by the need to add habit annotations the matrices usually lack.

operationalization: Measure external morphological similarity, ecological similarity and phylogenetic distance jointly, and test whether distant lineages in similar conditions converge in external form while remaining distant on an independent tree. The claim is confirmed if ecology predicts external resemblance after phylogeny is controlled, and refuted if external resemblance is explained by relatedness alone.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic distance used to show that externally similar species can be genealogically remote.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological characters for separating external, habit-related resemblance from internal structure.

candidate_datasets.name: TRY Plant Trait Database
candidate_datasets.role: Plant functional traits and habitats for cases such as succulent or aquatic form arising in unrelated families.

obstacles: External form is coded differently in each matrix, so a global resemblance score has to be harmonized.
Some apparent convergence is retained deep homology that a coarse ecological label misclassifies.
Similar climate is only a proxy for the 'similar conditions' that actually shaped the external parts.
rationale: External similarity, habitat and phylogenetic distance are all measured variables, and molecular trees are independent of the external form being judged. Public trees, morphological matrices and plant trait data cover enough classic and systematic cases to accept or reject the pattern, with plants and invertebrates less evenly coded than vertebrates. The confounding issues are real and are the ordinary ones of comparative methods, not a barrier to a decision.

operationalization: Through the Phanerozoic, test whether clades that are already species-rich and widespread tend to gain further species while smaller clades decline, and whether that replacement produces the observed concentration of diversity in few higher taxa. The claim is confirmed if prior richness and occupancy predict subsequent expansion and extinction of smaller groups beyond a constant-rate null, and refuted if clade success is independent of prior dominance.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Genus and species occurrences through time for richness, occupancy and replacement among higher taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Living diversity per clade, to score how concentrated species are in a few large groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Species totals for living orders and classes whose imbalance the mechanism is meant to explain.

obstacles: Constant-rate speciation and extinction already produce a few dominant clades, so imbalance alone does not show that large groups supplant small ones.
The pull of the recent and better preservation of young rocks make living groups look more dominant than they were.
Linking one group's gain to another group's extinction requires co-occurrence and interaction evidence the fossil record rarely has.
rationale: Richness, occupancy and extinction through time are in the fossil-occurrence record, so the expansion-and-replacement half can be tested for marine animals. The further claim that this is why all life falls into a few classes is a historical explanation that the same imbalance would suggest under simpler models. A null-model analysis is feasible and would remain ambiguous about the mechanism.

operationalization: Define phylogenetically isolated groups by long stem branches or high evolutionary distinctiveness, independently of their living species count, then test whether they have unusually few species, unusually large gaps among those species, and richer extinct membership. The claim is confirmed if isolation predicts species poverty and within-group disparity beyond a birth-death null and fossils show former richness, and refuted if isolated groups are not species-poor or show no sign of lost diversity.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Stem lengths and evolutionary distinctiveness used to identify aberrant groups without using their species counts.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Living species counts per genus and family.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinct diversity of groups that are species-poor today, as evidence of past loss.

obstacles: Under ordinary speciation and extinction, long-branched groups are often species-poor by chance, so poverty is not by itself evidence of a failed group.
Calling a group aberrant because its species are very distinct, and then treating that distinctness as a result, is circular unless fossils or an independent isolation measure is used.
The fossil record of the relevant stem groups is strong for some vertebrates and poor for most aberrant invertebrates and plants.
rationale: Isolation, richness and fossil diversity can be measured separately, which avoids defining aberrant groups by the very poverty being tested. Trees and occurrence databases cover living isolation well and past richness unevenly. A birth-death null is essential and is also the reason the pattern, even if found, only partly discriminates relict status from passive rarity.

operationalization: When a species shares characters with a distant group, map those characters on an independent tree and ask whether they are ancestral for the distant group or shared uniquely with one of its species. The claim is confirmed if such cross-group similarities are usually general plesiomorphies, and refuted if they usually match derived characters of a single species.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Matrices that record the characters underlying supposed cross-group affinities.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees on which those characters can be mapped as ancestral or as special to one terminal.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular data for a tree that does not depend on the morphological affinity being tested.

obstacles: Pre-cladistic 'affinity' mixes ancestral resemblance with convergence, so the characters to map are not uniquely defined.
Many matrices were assembled in order to resolve these same affinities, which makes the mapping partly circular.
The living members of a group are an incomplete sample of the ancient parent group whose characters the claim invokes.
rationale: Character mapping can separate a general resemblance to a group from a special resemblance to one species, which is the empirical contrast in the sentence. The required matrices exist for scattered taxa rather than for every cross-group affinity Darwin had in mind. Months of character coding would still leave a moderate risk that the result restates how the characters were chosen.

operationalization: For vertebrate classes and other well-fossilized higher groups, test whether stem fossils occupy morphological positions between the living classes and whether denser sampling shrinks the gaps. The claim is confirmed if connecting series are present and stratigraphically early, as with the dinosaur-bird transition, and refuted if a densely sampled class boundary shows a persistent morphological break with no intermediate stem forms.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrences and ages of stem fossils that would fill gaps between higher groups.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Morphological matrices placing fossil and living taxa in a common character space.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic framework for distinguishing stem connectors from members of the living crown groups.

obstacles: Soft-bodied and microscopic groups rarely preserve the intermediate anatomies the claim requires, so the test is strongest for skeletonized vertebrates.
A fossil can narrow a gap without showing that the missing forms were utterly destroyed rather than still unfound.
Last appearances are smeared backward by incomplete sampling, which can exaggerate how suddenly a connecting series seems to end.
rationale: Intermediate stem fossils are a direct confirming observation, and public occurrence data plus morphological matrices already contain the vertebrate series the claim highlights, including birds. A well-sampled class boundary with no intermediates would count against the claim, so the outcome can go either way. Non-vertebrate classes are less adequate, but they do not block a decision for the vertebrate scope Darwin treats as the strong case.

operationalization: Represent homologous parts as connectivity graphs and test whether, within a class, adjacency order stays fixed while shape and size vary, using gene expression or developmental identity as the homology criterion. The claim is confirmed if transpositions of connection are absent across tetrapod limbs, arthropod limbs and floral organs, and refuted by well-supported reversals of anatomical order.

candidate_datasets.name: Uberon
candidate_datasets.role: An anatomical ontology that records connections among vertebrate parts.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D specimens from which shape change can be measured separately from connectivity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Comparative matrices of limb, mouthpart and floral characters across members of a class.

obstacles: Homology has often been defined by conserved connections, so a purely anatomical test can become circular.
Connectivity is coded in an ontology for vertebrate anatomy and is not a downloadable comparative matrix for insect mouthparts, crustacean limbs and flowers together.
Digit identity shifts and homeotic floral changes require an agreed homology standard before they count as transpositions.
rationale: A no-transposition rule is empirically sharp once parts are homologized independently of their connections. Public anatomy ontologies and specimen repositories cover vertebrate skeletons much better than the full list of organ systems in the claim. Turning those sources into a class-wide connectivity test is months of coding, so only a subset can be resolved with what is already structured.

operationalization: Reconstruct the ancestral arrangement of a class-level organ system from fossils and living species, and test whether subsequent changes are small steps in shape and size that leave connections intact. The claim is confirmed if stem fossils already show the shared pattern and later disparity accumulates gradually, and refuted if the common ancestor lacks the pattern or later change is concentrated in a few large jumps.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Stem-group fossils that can show whether the shared pattern was already present early.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Character matrices for ancestral-state reconstruction of limbs, mouthparts and similar systems.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Trees on which ancestral arrangements and subsequent amounts of change are reconstructed.

obstacles: Ancestral-state models assume a tree and a mode of change, so gradual modification is partly built into the method.
Fine stratigraphic series of slight steps are available for a few skeletonized lineages and missing for most organ systems.
The original use of the ancestral pattern is not recorded by the fossils that preserve its structure.
rationale: Presence of the shared pattern in stem fossils is testable, and public matrices and occurrences support it for mammal limbs and a few other systems. 'Slight successive steps' and the ancestral function are much harder, and reconstruction methods favor the gradual story they are asked to detect. The feasible result is a partial historical test for well-fossilized organ systems, not for every class.

operationalization: Test two linked predictions: earlier or less modified members of vertebrates, arthropods and flowering plants show more numerous repeated parts, and ancestral-state or fossil reconstructions give those progenitors many similar segments, vertebrae or leaf-like organs. The claim is confirmed if repetition declines along derived branches and stem fossils are highly repetitive, and refuted if repetition is unrelated to phylogenetic grade or stem fossils already show specialized, non-repeated organs.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Early vertebrate, arthropod and plant fossils whose repeated parts can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental-gene sequences used, cautiously, as evidence that serial organs share an inherited patterning system.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Matrices scoring segment, vertebral and floral-organ repetition across living and fossil taxa.

obstacles: 'Low or little-modified' has often been defined by the presence of many repeated parts, which builds the predicted pattern into the ranking.
A shared patterning pathway can be co-opted later, producing serial organs without an ancestor that already possessed many of them.
The relevant early fossils are incomplete, especially for soft segmentation and for the origin of floral organs.
rationale: Counts of repeated parts and their distribution on a tree are measurable, but the progenitor story needs a fossil or ancestral reconstruction that is only partly available. Existing fossil occurrences and matrices can test a subset of vertebrates and arthropods and are weak for the floral-leaf comparison. Circular definitions of 'low' and the co-option alternative keep discriminating power modest.

operationalization: Within classes, compare multivariate morphological or transcriptomic distances among species at matched embryonic stages and at adult stages, and test whether embryonic similarity is independent of habitat similarity. The claim is confirmed if embryos of a class cluster more tightly than adults and embryonic closeness does not track shared conditions, and refuted if adults are as similar as embryos or embryonic resemblance follows ecology.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental transcriptome time series for cross-species distances through ontogeny.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Imaged embryos and adults for morphometric distances in a limited set of vertebrates.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Class membership and relationships for choosing which species should be compared.

obstacles: Matched embryonic stages exist mainly for model vertebrates and a few insects, not for animals of a whole class.
Staging landmarks are not equivalent across phyla, so an 'early' stage in one group is not the same comparison in another.
Transcriptome studies often find a mid-development hourglass rather than uniform embryonic similarity, which the morphometric data must be allowed to show.
rationale: Embryo-versus-adult distance is a clear criterion, and public expression archives plus specimen imagery can support it for small sets of vertebrates. That is a restricted scope relative to animals within a class. The comparison can discriminate the claim from ecology-driven embryonic resemblance, but assembling comparable stages across more than a handful of species is slow specialist work.

operationalization: For free-living larvae, compare trait-environment fit and among-species morphological disparity at the larval stage with the same quantities in adults of the same species. The disparity clause is confirmed if allied larvae differ at least as much as their adults where larval ecology differs, and refuted if larvae remain more uniform than adults despite active, divergent habits; 'as perfect' has no separate numerical threshold.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Larval and adult habitat and morphology for fishes, the best-tabulated free-living larvae.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Larval and adult character matrices for crustaceans, insects and related groups.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic and taxonomic context for allied species whose larvae and adults can be paired.

obstacles: 'As perfect and as beautiful' does not name a measurement that a dataset could fail.
Larval and adult disparity are comparable only when both stages are scored on the same characters, which is uncommon.
Larval ecology is tabulated for many fishes and for a few insect and crustacean groups, not for free-living larvae in general.
rationale: The disparity comparison is a genuine empirical clause and can be attempted for fishes and some arthropods with existing trait tables and matrices. The perfection clause has no decision threshold that preserves the wording, which caps operationalizability and discriminating power. Available data therefore test a proxy in a subset of taxa, and only that proxy.

operationalization: For dog, horse and pigeon breeds, compare multivariate distances among breeds at neonatal or juvenile stages and at adulthood on the same landmarks, excluding or separately noting early-appearing exceptions such as the short-faced tumbler. The claim is confirmed if among-breed distance increases with age for the breed-diagnostic proportions, and refuted if neonates already differ as much as adults across those breeds.
obstacles: Age-by-breed measurements exist as scattered veterinary and pigeon studies, not as one open morphometric table.
Breed standards and show data describe adults, so the juvenile half has to be recovered from separate growth papers.
Body size and allometry change proportions within a breed as it grows, and must be separated from true among-breed divergence.
rationale: The age contrast in proportions is directly measurable and would clearly confirm or refute the claim for these three domesticated species. The obstacle is data organization: published growth series would have to be compiled study by study, and they cover some dog and horse breeds far better than a balanced sample of pigeon breeds. That is a restricted, paper-by-paper test rather than an analysis of an existing public dataset.

operationalization: Compare trees or distance matrices built from embryonic characters with independent molecular trees, and compare both with trees built from adult characters. The claim is confirmed if groups that share embryonic stages are clades on the molecular tree more reliably than adult similarity would indicate, and refuted if embryonic similarity groups species that molecular data place far apart.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular trees that provide a descent criterion independent of embryonic characters.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Embryonic and larval character matrices, including classic cases such as cirripede larvae.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental expression profiles as a second, non-anatomical measure of embryonic similarity.

obstacles: Using embryonic similarity both to classify a group and to prove its common descent is circular unless the tree is molecular.
The most conserved developmental stage is often mid-embryogenesis rather than the earliest embryo, so 'the embryo' is not a single comparable object.
Comparative embryology matrices exist for scattered groups, not for animal groups in general.
rationale: Concordance between embryonic characters and molecular clades is a workable reading of embryonic structure revealing descent, and it can be checked wherever both exist. That intersection is a subset of animal groups, with barnacles and vertebrates far better documented than the rest. The molecular comparison avoids using the embryonic characters twice, but sparse matrices keep the test partial.

operationalization: Place fossil adults and the embryos and adults of their living relatives in one morphospace and test whether the fossils fall closer to the embryos than to the living adults. The claim is confirmed if stem fossils are repeatedly more embryo-like than their living adult relatives, and refuted if they are as close, or closer, to the living adults across well-sampled clades.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Identities and ages of candidate ancestral or stem fossils to compare with living descendants.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D fossils and embryos from which a shared morphospace can be built for a few skeletal systems.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: Developmental series that define embryonic stages when anatomy alone does not supply a stage standard.

obstacles: Fossil adults and embryos of descendants are rarely landmarked in the same coordinate system.
A stem fossil is a side branch, so resemblance to an embryo need not mean it preserves the ancestor's adult form.
Early-acting changes, which the claim itself allows, remove the predicted resemblance and make a negative result ambiguous.
rationale: A morphospace distance from fossils to embryos versus living adults is a concrete criterion, and it can be built for a few skeletal systems that have both fossil scans and developmental series. Most clades lack that joint coverage, and side-branch fossils are an imperfect stand-in for ancestors. The comparison is informative where the landmarks exist and is not a general test across extinct life.

operationalization: Measure when, in ontogeny, differences among related species first appear in morphology and gene expression, and whether the genetic variants that distinguish them are expressed at that same later age. The claim is confirmed if species differences and their underlying variants are systematically late and embryos remain comparatively uniform, and refuted if most differences are already present at the earliest stages.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic expression series for timing when species differences appear.

candidate_datasets.name: Ensembl
candidate_datasets.role: Gene models and comparative annotation for variants whose expression timing can be checked.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Relationships among the species whose developmental schedules are compared.

obstacles: Early embryonic similarity can be produced by selection removing early variants, which yields the same pattern without variations originating late.
Expression-timing and mapping data exist for a handful of model animals, not for animals generally.
Showing that a variant is inherited at a corresponding age requires pedigrees or experimental crosses that are available for very few traits.
rationale: The timing of first appearance of species differences is measurable in public expression series for a few well-studied animals. That timing does not separate late origin of variation from early origin plus later inheritance or from selective removal of early changes. The mechanism as a general explanation of embryology is therefore only partly constrained by existing data, and extending it past model species would be a long compilation.

operationalization: Using an explicit definition of a rudimentary organ as a reduced homolog with little or no current function, estimate the fraction of species or higher taxa that bear at least one, with a pre-set threshold for 'extremely common'. The claim is confirmed if that fraction exceeds the threshold across animals and plants, and refuted if rudiments are confined to a small minority of taxa.
obstacles: No public dataset inventories rudimentary organs across animals and plants.
Functionlessness is disputed for many classic rudiments, so the objects to be counted are unstable.
'Extremely common' has no numerical boundary, which must be set before any count can decide the claim.
rationale: A taxonomic census with a pre-registered threshold would decide the frequency claim, but that census has not been assembled as a dataset. Narrative lists in the anatomical literature are too uneven to estimate a rate, and gene-loss catalogues would answer a different question about pseudogenes. The analysis cannot be run until the variables are collected and coded.

operationalization: Compare coefficients of variation within species, and evolutionary rates among close species, for rudimentary structures versus functional homologues of similar size. The claim is confirmed if rudiments are consistently more variable within species and more divergent among allies, and refuted if their variation matches that of functioning parts after size and measurement error are controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Repeated scans of reduced pelves, limbs and similar rudiments from which within-species variation can be measured for a few taxa.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Matrices that occasionally score polymorphic or reduced states across allied species.

obstacles: Small structures have larger relative measurement error, which can imitate high variation.
Age and allometry change the apparent size of a rudiment and have to be separated from individual variability.
Published samples concentrate on a few famous rudiments, so the result may not extend to rudimentary organs in general.
rationale: A coefficient-of-variation contrast with functional homologues is a direct test of the variability clause. Specimen repositories and matrices contain the raw material for a handful of skeletal cases and do not contain a compiled variability table. Measuring those scans is slow, and measurement error on small parts is a serious but addressable confound.

operationalization: For a pre-specified list of rudimentary organs, compare each organ's size relative to neighbouring parts in late embryos and in adults, including organs that are present in the embryo and absent in the adult. The claim is confirmed if relative size is larger in the embryo in nearly every case, and refuted by a substantial set of rudiments that are relatively larger in the adult or absent in the embryo.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: Ontogenetic series of skeletal specimens for measuring relative size of reduced elements before and after maturity.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: Published anatomical codings of embryonic and adult states for rudiments such as reduced teeth and limbs.

obstacles: Developmental series of rudiments are scattered through individual papers and are not a single analysis-ready table.
Relative size depends on which adjoining landmark is chosen, and that choice can change the ratio.
Organs that appear only as embryonic buds, such as tooth germs, are mostly in histological collections rather than in public 3D archives.
rationale: Embryo-versus-adult relative size is an unambiguous measurement, and a modest number of counterexamples would challenge a claimed universal rule. Public scans and matrices cover some skeletal rudiments and miss most soft or transient ones. The decision criterion is strong; the missing compilation of developmental series is what limits the test to a subset.

operationalization: Across independent origins of cave life and island flightlessness, test whether organs that are unused in the derived habitat are reduced relative to their closest surface or flying relatives, and whether the reduction is greater in adults than in embryos. The association can be confirmed or refuted; inheritance of the effects of disuse is not separated by that comparison from relaxed selection or selection against a costly organ.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenies for counting independent origins of cave taxa and flightless island birds.

candidate_datasets.name: FishBase
candidate_datasets.role: Habitat and morphology fields for fishes, including subterranean species, as a partial source for eye and pigment loss.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: Species-level bird, mammal and reptile trees on which island and flight traits can be placed.

obstacles: Relaxed selection and positive selection for reduction predict the same association between disuse and smaller organs.
Studies of eye loss and flightlessness are concentrated on a few clades, so the sample of origins is narrower than the scope.
The embryonic-size consequence needs developmental series that these phylogenies and trait tables do not contain.
rationale: Repeated evolutionary loss of unused organs is testable with phylogenies and partial trait tables, and that association is the observable part of the claim. The further claim that disuse itself is the inherited cause is not distinguished by those data from selection or drift under relaxed function. Existing resources therefore resolve a proxy pattern for well-studied cases and leave the stated agency open.

operationalization: Take each traditional class of animals and plants as a set of included species and test whether those species form a single clade on a tree built from molecular characters. The claim is confirmed if each such class is monophyletic or is a single clade once historically excluded members are accounted for, and refuted if a class is composed of two or more unrelated clades.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A synthetic tree on which monophyly of each traditional class can be read directly.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genome-scale and marker sequences underlying class-level phylogenies.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Dated trees used to check that members of a class share an ancestor with each other rather than with other classes.

obstacles: Some traditional classes were defined by ecology or by the absence of traits and are paraphyletic, so membership has to be fixed from the historical concept before the test.
Horizontal gene transfer in fungi, plants and protists can make different genes disagree about a single progenitor for a class.
The deepest nodes of several invertebrate classes are still sensitive to taxon sampling and to the choice of model.
rationale: Monophyly of a named class is a standard phylogenetic question, and public trees already place most species that taxonomists assign to classes. Molecular data are largely independent of the morphological class diagnoses Darwin knew, which gives the test real discriminating power. Checking the historical membership of each class is days to weeks of work, not a new data collection.

operationalization: Count the smallest number of independent origins required by phylogenomic trees of animals and of plants, using explicit kingdom boundaries, and compare each count with five. The claim is confirmed if animals require at most five origins and plants require as few or fewer, and refuted if either kingdom is split into six or more unrelated clades.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genome and marker data for deep phylogenies of animals and of plant lineages.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global tree on which the number of separate animal and plant origins can be counted.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Conserved proteins used to test whether the deepest animal and plant groups share a single origin.

obstacles: The 1859 plant kingdom included fungi and several algal groups that are not one modern clade, so the plant total depends on that historical boundary.
Long-branch and compositional artefacts can still move deep nodes, although current genomic analyses do not divide animals into more than one origin.
An upper bound of four or five is easier to satisfy than an exact count, so a result of one origin confirms the inequality without testing why Darwin chose those numbers.
rationale: The number of independent origins is a direct tree question, and public genomes already resolve animals as a single clade, which meets an upper bound of four or five. The plant count is also low once plants are read as land plants or as Archaeplastida, and the main ambiguity is the broader 1859 kingdom rather than missing sequences. Recounting origins on existing trees is a short analysis.

operationalization: Across the major lineages of life, score shared nucleotide and amino-acid chemistry, cellular organization and a core of growth and reproductive processes, and test whether those features are present in essentially all organisms rather than in one kingdom. The claim is confirmed if the core is taxonomically universal, and refuted if substantial lineages lack cells or use an unrelated chemical basis of growth and reproduction.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Protein sequences documenting a shared amino-acid chemistry and conserved cellular machinery.

candidate_datasets.name: KEGG
candidate_datasets.role: Pathway maps for core metabolism, growth-related processes and reproductive or cell-cycle functions.

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Taxonomy
candidate_datasets.role: Taxonomic span of sequenced organisms used to check that the common features are not confined to animals or plants.

obstacles: 'Laws of growth and reproduction' is broader and vaguer than the chemical and cellular variables that databases actually tabulate.
A similar effect of the same poison on plants and animals is an incidental illustration and is not compiled for all lineages.
Shared chemistry would also be expected if independent origins had few viable chemical options, so universality alone is a weaker test of a single origin than of commonality.
rationale: Chemical composition and cellular machinery are directly tabulated for a wide taxonomic span, and absence of that core in a sequenced lineage would refute the empirical claim. Pathway and protein databases cover the chemical and cellular clauses well and the vague 'laws of growth' only by proxy. The comparison is a standard survey of existing molecular databases and can be completed quickly.

operationalization: Test whether all extant organisms, and fossils that can be placed, share homologous core genes and a single rooted network of descent. The claim is confirmed for known life if those cores are universal and congruent, and refuted if a lineage has an unrelated genetic system; organisms that left no descendants remain outside the test.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Genomes used to ask whether a core of homologous genes is shared across life.

candidate_datasets.name: UniProt
candidate_datasets.role: Universal protein families whose phylogenies root extant organisms to one ancestral system.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: A global synthesis of how far a single genealogy extends through named life.

obstacles: Gene exchange at the root is compatible both with one primordial cell and with a community of exchanging forms.
A second origin that died out without descendants would not appear in genomes or in the fossil record of later life.
Universal chemistry is expected under common ancestry and is also expected if early chemical options were severely limited.
rationale: Public genomes can strongly test common ancestry of extant life, which is the part of the claim that has measurable descendants. They cannot show that every organism that ever lived, including any vanished independent origin, belonged to that same genealogy. The analysis of universal genes is standard; the scope phrase 'which have ever lived' is why the claim is only partly resolvable.

operationalization: Compare named varieties and named species for the presence of living morphological or genetic intermediates, and for other candidate distinctions such as reproductive isolation and genetic-cluster gaps. The claim is confirmed if the presence or absence of living intermediates is the only consistent separator, and refuted if species and varieties also separate cleanly by isolation or genetic distance once intermediates are held constant.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic records of named species and infraspecific taxa, including zones where intermediates might occur.

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Rank labels that mark which forms are currently treated as species and which as varieties.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Genetic proximity among close forms, as a check on whether rank tracks something besides living intermediates.

obstacles: Taxonomists already use living intermediates to decide variety versus species, so the contrast is partly the definition under test.
Reproductive isolation and genetic clusters are not fields in these taxonomic databases and would have to be joined from separate studies.
Fossil intermediates that would show species were formerly connected are unavailable for the great majority of living species pairs.
rationale: The proposed distinction can be compared with other species criteria only where ranks, geography and genetic data coincide, which is a subset of organisms. Because rank assignments already encode the presence of intermediates, a checklist test is weakly discriminating. The result can show how present ranks behave and cannot establish that former connection is the only difference.

operationalization: Partition rates of origination, extinction and phenotypic change through time into components associated with biotic variables and with physical variables such as climate, and ask which component is larger. The claim is confirmed if biotic context explains more organic change than concurrent physical change across timescales, and refuted if physical change dominates or the two are inseparable.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Origination, extinction and faunal change through geological time.

candidate_datasets.name: NOAA Paleoclimatology
candidate_datasets.role: Independent physical-climate series to set against the amount of organic change.

candidate_datasets.name: GloBI
candidate_datasets.role: Modern organism-to-organism interactions as a present-day analogue, not a deep-time interaction record.

obstacles: Who interacted with whom is rarely fossilized, so biotic drivers are inferred from diversity patterns rather than observed.
Climate, sea level and collecting intensity move together with apparent turnover, which confounds the partition.
Which factor looks stronger depends on the time bin, so a single 'most important' cause is sensitive to scale.
rationale: A variance partition of organic change into biotic and physical correlates is a fair operationalization, and fossil occurrences plus paleoclimate series support it for the physical side. Deep-time interactions themselves are largely absent, so the biotic term is a proxy. Existing data can address the contrast for some intervals and do not securely rank the causes for all of geological time.

operationalization: Between consecutive formations, measure faunal dissimilarity and the radiometrically dated time span, controlling for rock volume and collection effort. The claim is confirmed if organic turnover increases with elapsed time closely enough to rank the lengths of gaps, and refuted if turnover is uncorrelated with dated duration once sampling and facies are controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Fossil occurrences by formation for measuring organic dissimilarity between consecutive units.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Rock units, gaps and sampled sedimentary volume used to control the comparison.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: The numerical geologic time scale that supplies elapsed time independent of the fossils.

obstacles: A change of facies or of collecting effort can produce faunal turnover within a short span of time.
Formations are local, and 'consecutive' units on different continents are not a single global clock.
The claim already calls the measure imperfect, so only a weak or absent correlation with radiometric duration would refute it.
rationale: Turnover and radiometric duration are both public variables, and a positive controlled correlation is a direct test of using organic change as a clock. Occurrence databases and the numerical time scale cover the Phanerozoic well enough for a global marine test, with coarser coverage of terrestrial formations. Sampling and facies are serious confounds and are also standard covariates in this analysis, which a small team can run.

operationalization: Estimate origination, extinction and morphological rates in successive intervals from the origin of life to the present, and test whether rates are lower in the earlier, taxonomically poorer intervals. The claim is confirmed if early intervals are slower after sampling correction, and refuted if early rates are as high as or higher than later ones once rock availability is controlled.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Phanerozoic origination and extinction rates, the best-resolved part of the history.

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: Molecular divergence times whose implied rates can be compared between deep and shallow branches.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: Interval ages, including the very long Precambrian bins in which an early slowdown would have to appear.

obstacles: The first dawn of life, where the claim says change may have been extremely slow, has almost no fossil resolution of biological rates.
Molecular clocks pushed to the origin of life are dominated by the choice of model and calibration.
A poor early rock record produces the appearance of slow change even if the biological rate was high.
rationale: Rate-through-time methods exist and can be applied to Phanerozoic fossils and to molecular trees, which covers the later part of the history the claim is about. The earliest interval, which carries the strongest wording, is exactly where public data are weakest. Sampling can imitate a slow start, so a low early rate in current compilations would not cleanly confirm the biological claim.

operationalization: Compare the radiometric length of the fossiliferous timescale known in 1859, essentially the Phanerozoic, with the time from the earliest evidence of life to the present. The claim is confirmed if that then-known history is a small fraction of post-origin time, and refuted if the two durations are similar under the range of credible dates for first life.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: Numerical ages for the base of the Cambrian and for the length of the Phanerozoic.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: The span of the fossil record that corresponds to the history of life known when the claim was written.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: Ages of the oldest preserved rock units, used to place the earliest geological and fossil evidence on the same scale.

obstacles: 'Mere fragment' has no numerical cutoff, so a ratio near one sixth can be described in more than one way.
The age of the first organism is a range, from debated early isotopic signals to clearer later fossils.
The phrase 'history of the world as at present known' has to be read as the 1859 fossiliferous timescale, because the geological record known today already includes most of Earth's history.
rationale: Both durations are now numerical, and the Phanerozoic is several times shorter than the interval since the earliest widely discussed evidence of life. That comparison uses public time scales and fossil and rock ages and can be made in days. The soft point is the rhetorical threshold for 'fragment', which keeps discriminating power moderate even though the direction of the inequality is clear.

operationalization: On a phylogenetic tree, score each mental capacity on a common ordinal scale across animals and humans and test whether every capacity appears by intermediate stages rather than in a single jump. The claim is confirmed if each capacity has precursor states in related organisms or in the archaeological and fossil record, and refuted by a capacity whose first appearance has no structural or behavioral intermediate.
obstacles: Mental capacities are not measured on one scale across taxa, so published experiments cannot be stacked into a single analysis.
A missing intermediate can always be assigned to an untested or extinct species, which weakens refutation.
Brain-size and archaeological records do not resolve particular faculties such as language or abstraction.
rationale: Gradual acquisition would be testable if comparable cognitive scores existed across a phylogeny, and they do not exist as a public dataset. Scattered experiments and endocranial volumes cover a few faculties in a few clades and leave 'each mental power' unmeasured. Until those scores are collected on a common scale, the analysis cannot confirm or refute the claim.

operationalization: At successive fossil time slices, score which species or genera still have descendants several intervals later, and test whether survivorship and later diversification are concentrated in taxa that were common, widespread and members of already large groups. The claim is confirmed if those traits predict leaving descendants and most taxa leave none, and refuted if rare members of small groups persist as often as common members of dominant groups.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Occurrence counts, geographic spread and forward survivorship of fossil taxa across intervals.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Modern occupancy of widespread versus restricted species, as a living analogue of the same predictors.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Clade sizes used to identify the larger, dominant groups whose members are predicted to prevail.

obstacles: Widespread taxa are more likely to be collected again, which imitates higher survivorship.
True species-level ancestor-descendant links are usually unavailable, so the test is forced down to genus occupancy.
Later geological intervals are a proxy for the 'far future', and the length of that proxy changes the result.
rationale: The future-looking sentence has a clear retrospective translation, and fossil occurrences record occupancy, clade size and which taxa persist. That translation is a proxy, and sampling bias toward widespread genera is severe enough to limit discriminating power. The survivorship model itself is a standard paleobiological analysis that can be run on existing downloads.

operationalization: Search the post-Silurian and earlier fossil record for any interval in which all lineages disappear and later life is phylogenetically unconnected to what came before. The claim is confirmed if every extinction interval retains survivors that include the ancestors of later biotas, and refuted by a global barren gap followed by a biota with no genealogical connection to earlier organisms.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction magnitudes and the presence of survivors across geological intervals.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: Phylogenetic continuity of living groups back through named ancestors and stem relatives.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: The timescale of mass-extinction boundaries and of the pre-Silurian interval the claim reaches behind.

obstacles: A complete sterilization in the poorly fossiliferous Precambrian, followed by survival of one lineage, would be difficult to see.
Extinction percentages depend on species concepts and on how completely each interval was sampled.
The claim is a universal negative, so its strength is set by the worst-sampled interval rather than by the well-known mass extinctions.
rationale: Total biotic reboot versus continuity through survivors is detectable in principle, and public occurrence data show survivors across the major Phanerozoic extinctions, none of which is a global end of all lineages. Phylogenies of living groups likewise connect them to pre-Silurian ancestors without a second origin. Precambrian resolution is weaker, but it does not erase the Phanerozoic test the fossil record can already decide.

operationalization: No dataset result would confirm or refute a tendency of all bodily and mental endowments toward perfection, because perfection names no measurable variable and any gain, loss or stasis can be redescribed as fitting the organism's own conditions.
obstacles: Perfection has no scale on which a simpler parasite, a lost eye or an unchanged structure would count as a failure.
Relative adaptedness changes whenever the environment changes, so a long-term approach to a fixed perfection is undefined.
Complexity, efficiency and fitness are alternative quantities, and adopting any one of them replaces the claim.
rationale: The sentence states a direction toward perfection without a variable that existing or future datasets record. Proxy series of complexity or performance exist in the literature, and using them would test a different proposition. Outcomes in which organs are lost or in which organisms merely persist are compatible with the wording, so the claim does not discriminate among biological histories.

operationalization: Treat the listed laws as separate variables, heritability, environmentally associated variation, population increase, differential persistence, divergence and extinction, and ask which of them can be shown jointly in existing datasets. The package is only partly testable: heritability, rapid potential increase and extinction have dataset criteria, while inheritance of use and disuse and the claim that this list jointly produces all living diversity do not have one decision rule.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: Extinction and replacement of forms through time, one clause of the listed mechanism.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: Parent-offspring genetic continuity as a dataset reading of inheritance.

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: Geographic and demographic spread of living populations, a weak public proxy for high rates of increase.

obstacles: The sentence binds several mechanisms, including variability from use and disuse, into one cause of all diversity, and those pieces do not share a single confirming result.
Showing heritability or extinction in existing data leaves the joint production of the entangled bank untested.
A small team cannot compile a decisive analysis of every named law from current databases in weeks.
rationale: Some listed processes have ordinary dataset tests, and public sequences, occurrences and fossils speak to inheritance, distribution and extinction separately. The claim asserts that the whole list, taken together, produced living diversity, which is a program of research rather than one analysis. Discriminating power stays low because many different biological theories are compatible with the same broad list.
